---
title: Using rpix with an IDE
knitr:
  opts_chunk:
    collapse: true
    comment: '#>'
---

Most R users work in an IDE rather than a terminal: RStudio, Positron or VS Code, or an editor such as Emacs, Neovim or Zed. Install the IDE as usual; most IDEs aren't available as conda packages, or not in recent versions. Then let rpix point it at the R in your project's Pixi environment, when you set the project up:

```r
rpix::use_pixi(ide = "positron")
```

or later, for one IDE at a time, with `use_pixi_rstudio()`, `use_pixi_positron()`, `use_pixi_vscode()`, `use_pixi_emacs()`, `use_pixi_neovim()` or `use_pixi_zed()`.

Some settings are a matter of taste, such as VS Code's R console. rpix asks about them as it sets the IDE up. To answer in advance, e.g. in a script, give them as arguments, also to `use_pixi()`:

```r
rpix::use_pixi(ide = "vscode", console = "arf")
```

Whichever IDE you use, `rpix::pixi_sitrep()` checks that it runs the project's R, and suggests fixes if it doesn't.

## Positron

### Set up

```r
rpix::use_pixi_positron()
```

This turns on Positron's discovery of R in Pixi environments, and makes the R from the project's default environment Positron's default for the project, in `.vscode/settings.json`. `default_r = FALSE` leaves the default out.

### Every day

Open the project, and Positron (2026.10 or later) starts its R. With an older Positron, or `use_pixi_positron(default_r = FALSE)`, pick **R (Pixi: default)** in the interpreter picker once; Positron remembers it for the project. Either way, the environment is activated when R starts, on Windows too.

The default's path is for the operating system `use_pixi_positron()` ran on. On another one, Positron ignores it, so collaborators there pick **R (Pixi: default)** once.

### Another environment

Each of the project's environments is listed as its own R, e.g. **R 4.4.3 (Pixi: r44)**. Pick it in the interpreter picker, or run `rpix::pixi_switch("r44")`, which looks for interpreters again and opens the picker.

### If something's off

- **Positron starts another R.** Positron prefers the R you last picked in the project over the default. If you used another R there before setting up Pixi, pick **R (Pixi: default)** once.
- **R (Pixi: default) isn't listed.** Positron may still show the R installations it found before, even in a new project. Run **Interpreter: Discover All Interpreters** from the Command Palette. Restart Positron if you've only just turned on discovery.

## RStudio

### Set up

```r
rpix::use_pixi_rstudio()
```

This adds an `rstudio` task to `pixi.toml`, and creates an `.Rproj` file if the project doesn't have one.

### Every day

Start RStudio with the task, in a terminal in the project folder:

```sh
pixi run rstudio
```

RStudio picks its R when it starts, so it has to be started this way. The task starts a new RStudio even if one is already running, and opens the project.

On Windows, the task expects RStudio in `C:/Program Files/RStudio`. If it's somewhere else, change the path in `pixi.toml`.

### Another environment

From RStudio, run:

```r
rpix::pixi_switch("r44")
```

This starts a new RStudio with the environment's R, in the project. The first time, it can take a while to open. Close the old one when you're done with it.

From a terminal, `pixi run --environment test rstudio` works too, for environments that include the default feature, which the task belongs to.

### If something's off

- **RStudio uses another R.** You probably opened the project another way, e.g. by double-clicking the `.Rproj` file. Close RStudio and use `pixi run rstudio`.

## VS Code

### Set up

```r
rpix::use_pixi_vscode()
```

This adds the languageserver package to the environment, and points the [R extension](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=REditorSupport.r) at the environment's R, in the project's `.vscode/settings.json`. It works the same in the editors based on VS Code, such as VSCodium, Cursor and Windsurf: they read the same settings, and get the R extension from [Open VSX](https://open-vsx.org/extension/REditorSupport/r). A project set up once works in all of them.

When the R extension offers to install its sess package, accept: Pixi adds the packages sess needs, and sess, which isn't on conda-forge yet, installs into the environment without being recorded in `pixi.toml`.

### Another console

The R extension's console can be [arf](https://github.com/eitsupi/arf) or [radian](https://github.com/randy3k/radian), instead of R. `use_pixi_vscode()` asks which, or takes it as an argument:

```r
rpix::use_pixi_vscode(console = "arf")
```

This adds arf to the environment, and points `r.consolePath` at it, with `r.consoleArgs` telling it to start the environment's R.

### Every day

Open the project folder in VS Code. The R extension uses the environment's R, and the project's `.Rprofile` activates the environment.

On Windows, the environment's R only starts when the environment is activated, because it needs the environment's `Library\bin` folder on the `PATH`. So start VS Code from the project's environment:

```sh
pixi run code .
```

For VSCodium, Cursor or Windsurf, use `codium`, `cursor` or `windsurf` instead of `code`.

### Another environment

Run `rpix::pixi_switch("r44")`. It changes `r.executablePath` and `r.consolePath` in `.vscode/settings.json` to the environment's R, `${workspaceFolder}/.pixi/envs/r44/bin/R`. With arf or radian as the console, it keeps the default environment's console, and points it at the environment's R. Then run **Developer: Reload Window** from the Command Palette.

On Windows, start VS Code with `pixi run --environment r44 code .` instead (or `codium`, `cursor` or `windsurf`). The console then has to be in that environment too.

### If something's off

- **The R extension can't find R.** Check that the environment is installed (`pixi install`), and that the paths in `.vscode/settings.json` exist.
- **Positron and VS Code share `.vscode/settings.json`.** Each ignores the other's settings, so a project can be set up for both.

## Emacs, Neovim and Zed

These editors start R, and languageserver, from the `PATH`. [direnv](https://direnv.net) puts the environment's on it whenever you're in the project's folder.

### Set up

Install direnv once, with Pixi:

```sh
pixi global install direnv
```

Then, in the project:

```r
rpix::use_pixi_emacs()   # or use_pixi_neovim(), use_pixi_zed()
```

This adds the languageserver package to the environment, and a `.envrc` file that activates the environment (`rpix::use_pixi_direnv()` writes just the file). direnv only loads a `.envrc` you've allowed, and again after it changes: rpix offers to allow it, or run `direnv allow` in the project.

Each editor loads direnv in its own way:

- **Emacs:** install the [envrc](https://github.com/purcell/envrc) package and turn on `(envrc-global-mode)`. ESS, and languageserver through eglot or lsp-mode, then use the project's R.
- **Neovim:** start Neovim from a shell with [direnv's hook](https://direnv.net/docs/hook.html), or use a direnv plugin such as [direnv.vim](https://github.com/direnv/direnv.vim). [R.nvim](https://github.com/R-nvim/R.nvim) and languageserver then use the project's R.
- **Zed:** Zed loads direnv by itself. Install its R extension: languageserver then uses the project's R, and so does R in Zed's terminal.

On Windows, direnv is rarely available, and the environment's R only starts when the environment is activated. Start the editor from the environment instead: `pixi run emacs`, `pixi run nvim` or `pixi run zed .`.

### Another environment

Run `rpix::pixi_switch("r44")`. It points `.envrc` at that environment. Reload direnv in the editor (in Emacs, `M-x envrc-reload`; in Neovim, start it again from the project; in Zed, reopen the project), then restart R.

## The message at startup

If you start R in a Pixi project with an R that isn't from the project's environment, e.g. by double-clicking the `.Rproj` file, which opens your usual R, the project's `.Rprofile` says so, as long as rpix is installed in that R:

```
! This R isn't from the project's Pixi environment, so it doesn't use the project's packages.
ℹ Start R with `pixi run R`, or see https://roald-arboel.com/rpix/articles/ide.html.
```

Your usual R can't use the environment's packages: they're built for the environment's R, and loading them can crash another R. So rpix doesn't try; start the environment's R instead, as above.

## Check

In the IDE's R console, `R.home()` should be inside the project's `.pixi/envs/` folder:

```r
R.home()
#> [1] "/path/to/project/.pixi/envs/default/lib/R"
```
